opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the short answer is yes, but with some really important qualifications. The Bayesian picture captures something deep about what both children and scientists are doing. You have some prior beliefs about how the world works, you get new evidence, and you shift your beliefs in a rational way. Crucially, you don't just throw everything out the minute you see one surprising thing, but you also don't cling to your old ideas no matter what.

What we found in the lab is that even very young children, preschoolers and sometimes even babies, are remarkably sensitive to the statistics of the evidence they see. If you show a four-year-old a machine that lights up when you put certain blocks on it, they'll make quite sophisticated inferences about which blocks are causing it to go, and they'll take into account how probable those hypotheses were to begin with. That looks very much like Bayesian inference.

But here's the interesting twist. Children aren't just less-informed adults doing the same thing. In some ways they're better learners than we are, because their priors are weaker, and they're more willing to consider unlikely hypotheses. We found that when the right answer is an unusual one, four-year-olds will often get it when adults won't. Adults are stuck with their strong priors. In computational terms, children seem to be searching the space of hypotheses in a broader, noisier, more exploratory way, something like a high-temperature search, whereas adults do a more narrow, exploit-what-you-already-know kind of search.

So I'd say the Bayesian framework tells you what the right inferences are, but it doesn't tell you how you actually find the hypotheses to evaluate in the first place. And that's where childhood comes in. Childhood is this protected period where you get to explore, play, try out wild ideas, without having to worry about the consequences. That's what makes children like the research and development division of the human species, and adults more like production and marketing.

And scientists, at their best, are people who've managed to keep some of that childlike exploratory capacity, plus they have the institutions of science, which give them a kind of protected space to explore, the way childhood does for children. Of course, the irony is that scientists in practice are often much less Bayesian than children are, because they have careers and reputations invested in particular hypotheses.

r001.rationale: The response describes Bayesian inference in children and scientists but does not distinguish practical reasoning from answering explicit questions about that reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says Bayesian learners should not abandon their beliefs after one surprising observation, framing belief revision as a rational response to evidence.

r003.rationale: It says children can outperform adults on unusual hypotheses, but does not say they outperform scientists.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that a scientific community’s mix of people favoring existing priors and new evidence helps it reach the right answer.

r005.rationale: It offers no view on whether there is a universal rule for deciding when to abandon a scientific theory.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that "Bayesian" can mean a couple of different things, and it's worth separating them. There's the strong claim, which is that children or scientists are literally representing probability distributions and doing the arithmetic of Bayes' rule in their heads. Nobody really believes that, and I certainly don't. Then there's the weaker and I think much more interesting claim, which is that the pattern of learning you see looks the way it would look if someone were doing something like that — that you can characterize it in those terms, and that doing so lets you make predictions that turn out to be right.

So in that second sense, yes, I think children are remarkably good approximate Bayesian learners, and I'd say they're better at it in some respects than adults are. What we've found in the lab, over and over, is that if you give a four-year-old a set of data about, say, which blocks make a machine light up, they'll pick out the hypothesis that best accounts for that data, they'll weigh the prior plausibility of different causal structures against how well they fit the evidence, and — this is the part that's really striking — they'll revise. If you show them something that doesn't fit, they don't just dig in. They'll move to a less likely hypothesis if the evidence warrants it. Adults will often stick with what they already believe for longer than the data justifies.

The analogy to scientists is one I've been making for a long time, and I still think it's right, but I'd put it a particular way. It's not that children are little scientists in the sense of running controlled experiments with clipboards. It's that scientists are big children — that what science does institutionally, with its norms of testing and revision and openness to being wrong, is a formalized version of something that human children do spontaneously. Science works because it taps into a learning capacity that's already there very early in development.

Now, where I think the picture gets complicated — and where I've changed my thinking somewhat — is on the question of how children handle the search problem. Bayesian inference tells you how to weigh hypotheses you've already got, but it doesn't tell you where the hypotheses come from. And what looks to me like the real distinctive feature of childhood is that children are exploring a much wider hypothesis space than adults do. They're doing something closer to what computer scientists call high-temperature search — they try out a lot of odd possibilities, they're noisier, they're less exploitative. That's actually a feature, not a bug, if your job is to figure out how a new world works. Adults have narrowed down; we're very good at exploiting what we already know, and consequently we're worse at discovering genuinely new structure.

So my short answer is: children and scientists are both Bayesian in the sense that matters — they update rationally in response to evidence. But the thing that makes childhood special isn't the updating. It's the breadth of the search and the willingness to entertain hypotheses that an adult would have ruled out before even considering them.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes literal Bayes-rule calculation from learning patterns that resemble Bayesian updating, but does not contrast practical reasoning with answering explicit questions about that reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says adults may stick with beliefs longer than the evidence justifies, but does not explain when retaining a strongly supported prior despite limited contrary evidence is rational.

r003.rationale: It says children can be better than adults at some aspects of Bayesian learning, but does not claim they outperform scientists on unusual-outcome problems.

r004.rationale: It describes science as formalizing children's learning capacity, but says nothing about a scientific community combining people who favor existing priors with people who favor new evidence.

r005.rationale: It does not address whether there is a universal rule for deciding when to abandon a scientific theory.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the important distinction is between saying that children or scientists are literally sitting there calculating Bayes’ theorem, which they clearly aren’t, and saying that Bayesian inference gives us a good account of what they’re accomplishing when they learn.

The basic problem is that you have some evidence, but there are many possible explanations for it. You have to weigh what you already thought was plausible against what the new evidence tells you. Bayesian models let us make that problem precise. We can ask, if a child were considering these different hypotheses, how should seeing this particular event change what she believes? Then we can see whether children actually behave that way. And in a surprising range of cases, even very young children do.

But that leaves a further question, which is how they manage it. The space of possible explanations is enormous. Scientists don’t systematically consider every possible theory, and neither do children. They explore, try things out, and consider a few possibilities. So I think the interesting work is connecting that abstract account of good inference to the actual processes of play, experimentation, and discovery.

r002.rationale: It does not address retaining a strongly supported prior when faced with limited contrary evidence.

r003.rationale: It says young children often behave in line with Bayesian models, but does not compare children with scientists on unusual outcomes.

r004.rationale: It discusses exploration by children and scientists, but not how a scientific community’s mix of prior-favoring and evidence-favoring people could reach the right answer.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss whether there is a universal rule for abandoning a scientific theory.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it helps to distinguish two claims. One is that children and scientists literally sit there calculating Bayesian probabilities. That’s almost certainly not what children do, and it’s not what scientists do most of the time either. The other is that Bayesian inference gives us a way of describing how you could learn about the world by combining what you already believe with new evidence.

What’s striking about children is that they seem to do more than just register that one thing follows another. They construct hypotheses about how the world works, and then they change those hypotheses in light of what they see. In experiments, you can show that even very young children are sensitive to how probable the evidence would be under different causal explanations.

But the interesting question is how they actually manage this. You can’t consider every possible hypothesis. So you need ways of generating possibilities and exploring them. I think children’s play and scientists’ experiments are particularly interesting here: they’re ways of getting evidence that you wouldn’t get by simply watching the world go by. Bayesian models give us a useful framework, but they don’t, by themselves, settle the question of what the underlying psychological processes are.
